mappings.note: Use four idioms from the text in sentences of your own. The skill is knowing what the idiom means, so C-E1.1 vocabulary rather than a writing-format outcome.
Why starting a diary felt strange to Anne is part of explaining why she begins one at all; LO-3 covers that, while LO-5 is about the honesty a diary permits.
'Paper has more patience than people' is precisely the claim that a diary allows an openness other writing and other listeners do not - LO-5, not LO-3's question of why she started.
She sketches her life because Kitty would not follow her stories otherwise; the answer turns on the invented listener, which is LO-4.
'What tells you' requires the learner to find the detail in the text that proves the feeling - textual evidence, LO-3, rather than a supplied quotation to interpret.
Both halves are stated facts: he was annoyed at her talking and set the 'Chatterbox' essay. Retrieval, LO-1.
Anne's argument in the essay is reported in the text, so the answer is extracted rather than constructed; LO-1.
A verdict on Mr Keesing as a teacher - character analysis, LO-2. The diary-specific C-E1.2 outcomes do not reach him.
What changed Mr Keesing's mind is about his character softening, LO-2, not a plain event.
Asks the learner to judge Anne's own prediction against what became of the diary - an opinion argued from outside the text, so the general C-E1.2 rather than one of its diary-specific LOs.
'In what way is Anne's diary different' is the honesty claim of LO-5; the language it was written in (Dutch) is a retrievable fact, LO-1.
Explicitly asks whether Kitty is treated as an insider or an outsider - the invented-listener question, LO-4.
Matches journal, diary, log and memoir to their definitions. Terminology and word meaning, C-E1.1.
Applies those definitions to four sample entries, which means reading each for register and purpose - conceptual understanding and inference, C-E1.1, not producing a piece of writing.
Locates phrasal verbs in the text and matches them to meanings. Vocabulary, C-E1.1; the items are lexical rather than structural, so not C-E1.3.
Second half of the same phrasal-verb matching exercise (its stored answer has been corrupted with an unrelated play extract). Vocabulary, C-E1.1.
Keep a diary for a week using diary language - subjectless sentences, contractions, everyday expressions. That is LO-6, writing one's own entries in Anne's tone and format.
Completes a ten-blank summary of a Samuel Pepys extract. Extracting stated information from a prose passage, LO-1.
MCQ version of why the diary felt a strange undertaking to Anne - her reasons for beginning it, LO-3.
Gives the meaning of the idiom 'your heart goes out to somebody'. Vocabulary, C-E1.1.
Finds contracted forms in the text and expands the ambiguous ones (I'd = I had / I would). Contraction is a grammatical convention, C-E1.3, not a lexical item.
Anne's feelings towards four people, and what they reveal about her - character analysis, LO-2.
The content of the first essay is reported in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
Tests Anne's claim about unpredictable teachers against Mr Keesing's behaviour - character in context, LO-2.
Five quotations are supplied and the learner must say what each shows about Anne. The evidence is given, so this is character analysis (LO-2) rather than the evidence-finding of LO-3.
The name Kitty is stated in the text; single-fact retrieval, LO-1.
MCQ version of why she sketches her family - so the imagined reader can follow her. The invented listener, LO-4.
Maths as the doubtful subject is stated; retrieval, LO-1.
Her talkativeness as the cause of his annoyance is stated outright; retrieval, LO-1.
The essay titles Mr Keesing set are named in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
MCQ version of the argument in her essay (an inherited trait). Stated in the text, so LO-1.
Why she cannot get close to her friends - she cannot bring herself to speak of personal things - is about who she is, LO-2, rather than about the diary itself.
The number of teachers is a stated figure; retrieval, LO-1.
The essay title 'A Chatterbox' is named in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
Sanne's gift for poetry is a stated detail; retrieval, LO-1.
The duck-family poem of the third assignment is described in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
Mr Keesing's name and subject are stated; single-fact retrieval.
Recall that the diary itself is her true friend. The item only asks for the fact, so LO-1, whereas explaining why she needs an invented listener would be LO-4.
Her father's age at marriage is a stated figure in the family sketch; retrieval, LO-1.
The punishment was an essay - a stated fact; retrieval, LO-1.
